Inside a <template>, top-level refs are unwrapped automatically, so you write {{ count }}.

Why const works. If count is const, how can its value change?

javascript
const count = ref(0) count.value = 5 // OK: mutating the .value property of the existing object count = ref(10) // ERROR: count cannot be reassigned

const only prevents the variable from being pointed at a different object; it says nothing about the contents of the object. The binding never needs to change, only the value stored inside it, which is why const is the convention for ref.

reactive makes an object deeply reactive without .value:

javascript
import { reactive } from 'vue' const user = reactive({ name: 'John', role: 'Engineer' }) user.name = 'Jane' // reactive, no .value needed

Caveats: it only works for objects (not primitives), and you lose reactivity if you reassign the whole variable or destructure it. Many developers use ref for everything.

9.5Interpolation and expressions

{{ ... }} ("mustache") inserts a JavaScript expression result as text.

javascript
{{ name }} {{ getPhone() }} {{ 'Mr ' + name }} {{ 1 + 2 }} {{ name.toUpperCase() }} {{ number + 1 }} {{ ok ? 'YES' : 'NO' }} {{ message.split('').reverse().join('') }} <div :id="`list-${id}`"></div>

[wk4 Example2.vue; wk5 Example2.vue].

Expressions only [Wk5 slides "Using JavaScript Expressions (2)"]: an expression is anything that can go after return. Statements do not work.

javascript
{{ var a = 1 }} <!-- WRONG: statement --> {{ if (ok) { return message } }} <!-- WRONG: flow control; use a ternary --> {{ ok ? message : '' }} <!-- RIGHT -->
  • Mustaches cannot go inside an HTML attribute. <img src="{{ url }}"> is wrong; use :src="url" (§7.8) [Wk4 slides "Attribute Binding (1)"].
  • v-html renders a string as raw HTML. The lab tests penalise unnecessary v-html by 1 mark per occurrence [LT26 Instructions]. Use {{ }} for text; v-html only when you really must show HTML markup (the slide examples use it for prod.desc that contains <p> tags).

Expressions, statements and v-html in detail

  • Expression: a piece of code that produces a value, e.g. score + 1.
  • Statement: a piece of code that performs an action but does not produce a value, e.g. if (score > 50) { console.log('Pass') }.

{{ }} evaluates a single expression and inserts the result as text. By default it escapes its result, so HTML tags are shown literally:

vue
<script setup> import { ref } from 'vue' const message = ref('<em>Warning</em>') </script> <template> <p>{{ message }}</p> <!-- shows the literal text <em>Warning</em> --> <p v-html="message"></p> <!-- parsed as HTML: italic Warning --> </template>

Security: cross-site scripting (XSS). v-html inserts a value as raw HTML. If message contains content typed by a user, they can insert their own HTML and JavaScript into the page. {{ }}'s default escaping exists specifically to prevent this. Use v-html only when the source is fully trusted, never on unvalidated user input.

lessons.goal: v-if, v-bind, v-on, v-model and v-for.
lessons.subtitle: v-if, v-bind, v-on, v-model and v-for.

🗺️ In this chapter
1Directive overview→2Conditional rendering: v-if, v-else-if, v-else→3Binding attributes, classes and styles: v-bi…→4Events: v-on / @→5Form input binding: v-model→6Lists: v-for
10.1Directive overview

Directives are attributes with a v- prefix. They apply effects to the DOM when the value of their expression changes [Wk4 slides "Vue Directives"].

Directive Shorthand Does Section
v-bind:attr="x" :attr="x" bind an attribute, class or style to a variable §7.8
v-on:event="x" @event="x" listen to a DOM or custom event §7.9
v-model="x" none two-way binding of a form input to a variable §7.10
v-if / v-else-if / v-else none insert or remove an element §7.7
v-for="item in items" none repeat an element per item §7.11
v-html="x" none render a string as HTML (avoid) §7.5
v-slot:name #name (added context) fill a named slot §7.14

Diagram: choosing the right tool.

I need to…Use
Show or hide somethingv-if / v-else
Repeat per array itemv-for + :key
Set an attribute, class or stylev-bind or :
React to click / key / mousev-on or @
Read a form inputv-model
Value derived from other datacomputed()
Side effect when data changeswatch()
Run code once on loadonMounted()

Ask the questions in any order; each answer gives one tool. Most lab questions combine three or four of these.

10.2Conditional rendering: v-if, v-else-if, v-else

What / when: the element is inserted or removed from the DOM depending on a truthy expression. Use it for "show X only when Y", empty-list messages and error banners [Wk4 slides "Conditional Rendering"].

vue
<p v-if="x == 1">Now you see me</p> <p v-else-if="x == 2">Second case</p> <p v-else>You don't see me</p> <!-- toggle several elements at once: <template> is an invisible wrapper, it is NOT rendered --> <template v-if="ok"> <h1>Title</h1> <p>Paragraph 1</p> </template> <template v-else> <p>Now you don't</p> </template>

[wk4 Example3.vue, Example4.vue; wk5 Ex2.vue solution].

  • v-else must come immediately after its v-if or v-else-if element, or Vue does not recognise it.
  • The condition must be a reactive variable to update [Wk4 slides].
  • v-if vs v-show (added context): v-show only toggles CSS display:none; v-if really adds/removes. Prefer v-if (it is what the course uses).

Empty-list pattern (2026 Q3 Part C) [LT26 q3.vue]:

html
<p v-if="collectionLogs.length === 0">No collection records yet</p> <table v-else> ... </table>

v-if vs v-show

v-if v-show
Element when the condition is false Removed from the page entirely Present, but hidden with display: none
Cost of toggling Recreates the element each time Only toggles a CSS property
Supports v-else Yes No
Best suited to Content that rarely changes visibility Content that toggles visibility frequently

A v-else-if chain is checked top to bottom and only the first true branch renders. With score = 72 in v-if="score >= 90" (Distinction) / v-else-if="score >= 70" (Merit) / v-else-if="score >= 50" (Pass) / v-else (Fail), the Merit branch renders and the rest are not evaluated further. If another element sits between a v-if and its v-else, Vue cannot associate the two and reports an error.

10.3Binding attributes, classes and styles: v-bind / :

What / when: anywhere an HTML attribute's value should come from a variable: src, href, id, width, value, disabled, class, style. Shorthand : is the norm [Wk4 slides "Attribute Binding"].

vue
<img v-bind:src="myImg" :width="width" :height="height" /> <!-- bind several attributes with ONE object --> <script setup> const obj = ref({ width: 200, height: 200, src: '/assets/me.png' }) </script> <img v-bind="obj" />

[wk4 Ex2.vue solution].

Boolean attributes (disabled, checked) exist by presence. Bind them to a true/false:

html
<button :disabled="isButtonDisabled">Log In</button> <input type="checkbox" v-bind:checked="isChecked"> <!-- disable a button until BOTH inputs are filled (2026 Q3 idea) --> <button :disabled="studentName.trim() === '' || selectedSize === ''">Collect</button>

[wk4 Example6.vue; LT26 q3.vue].

Class binding [wk4 Example8.vue]. Notice the quotes around class names containing a hyphen ('text-danger'), because a hyphen is a minus sign in JavaScript.

html
<!-- Object: key = class name, value = condition --> <p :class="{ active: isActive, 'text-danger': hasError }">{{ message }}</p> <!-- Static + dynamic mix --> <div class="static" :class="{ demo: isActive, 'text-danger': hasError }"></div> <!-- Array: apply a list of class names held in variables --> <div :class="[activeClass, errorClass]"></div> <!-- Computed object (wk5 Example6.vue) --> const classObject = computed(() => ({ active: isActive.value && !error.value, 'text-danger': error.value })) <div :class="classObject">Example</div> <!-- Two-way switch between two classes (wk4 Ex4.vue solution) --> <div :class="{ blueBox: blueBox, redBox: !blueBox }"></div> <button :class="{ btn: true, 'btn-primary': blueBtn, 'btn-danger': !blueBtn }"></button>

Yes/No coloured cells (2026 Q4 Part D) use the same idea with the given classes:

html
<td :class="course.coreForIS ? 'text-yes' : 'text-no'">{{ course.coreForIS ? 'Yes' : 'No' }}</td>

Style binding takes an object of CSS properties. Use camelCase (fontSize) or quoted kebab ('font-size') [wk4 Example9.vue]:

html
<p :style="{ color: activeColor, fontSize: size }">Inline styling</p> <div :style="{ color: activeColor, fontSize: fontSize + 'px' }"></div> <!-- numbers need units --> <div :style="{ 'font-size': fontSize + 'em' }"> <!-- [wk6 Example5View.vue] -->

Ordinary, boolean and merged bindings

Template Result
<a :href="link"> Sets href to the value of link
<button :disabled="isLoading"> Sets disabled based on isLoading
<input :id="fieldId"> Sets id to the value of fieldId

v-bind:src="imageUrl" sets the attribute to the current value and updates it whenever the variable changes: the same automatic behaviour as {{ }}, applied to an attribute instead of text content.

Boolean attributes (disabled, checked, readonly): in plain HTML you cannot write disabled="false" to mean "not disabled"; only the attribute's presence matters. v-bind handles this for you: when the bound value is false, null or undefined, Vue removes the attribute from the element entirely rather than writing the word "false" into it.

html
<button :disabled="isLoading">Submit</button> <!-- isLoading true: rendered with `disabled`, button inactive. isLoading false: the disabled attribute is removed, button clickable again. -->

Static and bound classes merge (neither overwrites the other):

html
<div class="card" :class="{ active: isActive }">Item</div>
isActive Rendered class attribute
true class="card active"
false class="card"

The array form :class="[baseClass, themeClass]" is useful when a set of classes should always be applied or is built up from several sources.

10.4Events: v-on / @

What / when: run code when the user does something (click, type, hover) [Wk5 slides "Event Handling"]. @click is short for v-on:click.

vue
<script setup> import { ref } from 'vue' const counter = ref(0) const name = ref('Vue') function hello(event) { // Vue passes the native DOM event automatically alert('Hello ' + name.value + '!') alert(event.target.tagName + ' event!') // BUTTON } function say(message) { alert(message) } </script> <template> <button v-on:click="counter += 1">Add 1</button> <!-- inline expression --> <button v-on:click="hello">Say Hello</button> <!-- method name: NO parentheses, event auto-passed --> <button @click="say('hi')">Say hi</button> <!-- method with your own argument --> <input type="text" v-on:keyup.enter="say('You pressed enter!')"> <div :id="id" @mouseover="mOver" @mouseout="mOut">Mouse Over Me</div> </template>

[wk5 Example1.vue; Ex1.vue solution].

  • Key modifiers: .enter, .tab, .delete (Delete and Backspace), .esc, .space, .up, .down, .left, .right.
  • Events listed on the slide: click, change, input, mouseover, mouseout, keypress, load (also submit, focus, keyup are mentioned).
  • Inline handlers may contain statements (counter += 1, isButtonDisabled = true); mustaches may not.
  • @submit.prevent="save" stops a form reloading the page (added context; .prevent, .stop are standard modifiers not shown in the slides).

@click="hello()" calls hello with no event; @click="hello" passes the event. If you need both, write @click="hello($event, 5)" (added context). Forgetting .value when a handler changes a ref is the #1 "my button does nothing" cause.

Events, modifiers and $event in detail

Event Fires when
@click The element is clicked
@input The value of a text field changes
@submit A form is submitted
@keyup A key is released while the element is focused
@mouseover The pointer moves over the element

@ works with any standard DOM event. A handler referenced without parentheses (@click="increment") is given to Vue as a function reference and Vue calls it when the event fires; it receives the event object automatically as its first argument.

vue
<script setup> import { ref } from 'vue' const message = ref('') function showGreeting() { message.value = 'Hello there' } </script> <template> <button @click="showGreeting">Greet</button> <p>{{ message }}</p> </template>

To pass both your own value and the event, call the handler explicitly and use the special variable $event, which stands in for the event object Vue would have passed:

vue
<script setup> function removeItem(id, event) { console.log('Removing item', id) console.log('Triggered by', event.type) } </script> <template><button @click="removeItem(42, $event)">Remove</button></template>

Event modifiers (attached to the event name):

Modifier Effect
.stop Stops the event from propagating to parent elements
.prevent Prevents the browser's default action for that event
.once The handler runs only on the first occurrence
.self The handler only runs if the event originated on this exact element, not a child
html
<form @submit.prevent="handleSubmit"> <!-- stops the page reload --> <button type="submit">Send</button> </form> <a @click.stop.prevent="handleClick">Link</a> <!-- chained, applied in the order written -->

Without .prevent, handleSubmit still runs, but the browser also reloads the page immediately afterwards, discarding application state. @click.stop.prevent stops the click propagating to parents and separately prevents the default handling (such as following the link's href).

@keyup.enter="search" runs search only when the released key is Enter, not after every character. Other key modifiers: .esc, .tab, .space, each named after its key.

10.5Form input binding: v-model

What / when: two-way binding between an input and a variable: typing updates the variable, and changing the variable updates the input. Use it on <input>, <textarea> and <select> [Wk4 slides "Form Input Binding"; Wk5 slides].

vue
<script setup> import { ref } from 'vue' const message = ref('Hello') const checked = ref(false) // single checkbox: boolean const selectedFruits = ref([]) // several checkboxes: array const picked = ref('') // radio group: one value const selected = ref('') // select: one value </script> <template> <input v-model="message" placeholder="edit me"> <textarea v-model="message"></textarea> <input type="checkbox" id="checkbox" v-model="checked"> <label for="checkbox">Checked? {{ checked }}</label> <!-- checkboxes bound to the SAME array collect their value attributes --> <input type="checkbox" value="Apple" v-model="selectedFruits"> Apple <input type="checkbox" value="Orange" v-model="selectedFruits"> Orange <input type="radio" name="num" value="One" v-model="picked"> One <input type="radio" name="num" value="Two" v-model="picked"> Two <select v-model="selected"> <option disabled value="">Please select one</option> <option>A</option> <option>B</option> </select> </template>

[wk5 Example4.vue].

Dynamic values (v-model + v-bind:value) [wk5 Example5.vue]:

html
<input type="radio" v-model="pick" :value="a"> A <!-- value comes from the variable a --> <select v-model="selected"> <option v-for="option in options" :value="option.value">{{ option.text }}</option> </select>

Modifiers:

Modifier Effect Example
.number typecast input to a Number <input v-model.number="age"> ([wk5 Ex3.vue]: x, y in a calculator)
.trim trim whitespace <input v-model.trim="msg"> ([LT26 q3.vue])

(added context: an <input type="number"> is converted to a number automatically; .number matters for type="text".)

v-model vs v-bind: v-bind is one-way (variable to attribute). v-model is shorthand for v-bind:value="x" plus v-on:input="x = $event.target.value" [Wk5 slides "v-model vs v-bind"].

  • Radio buttons in one group must share v-model and name; each needs a distinct value.
  • Multi-select checkboxes need an array (ref([])), a single checkbox needs a boolean. A ref('') used for a single checkbox holds '' instead of true/false (see checked in [wk5 Example4.vue], it works but starts as a string).
  • Put disabled value="" on the first <option> to make a "Please select" placeholder that cannot be re-chosen.
  • Every input you read later needs its own v-model variable; declare the ref in <script setup> first. In the 2026 Q4 starter, addCourse() reads newCode.value etc. but they are not declared, you must add them.

What v-model binds, per element

v-model adapts to the element it sits on, binding the property and event that make sense for it:

Element Property bound Event listened to Stores
<input type="text">, <textarea> value input The typed text
<input type="checkbox"> checked change Single box: true / false. Several boxes sharing one array: the value of every ticked box
<input type="radio"> checked change The value of the selected button
<select> value change The value of the chosen <option>

v-model modifiers

Modifier Effect
.lazy Updates the state on change (field loses focus or Enter is pressed) instead of on every keystroke
.number Converts the input to a number before storing it
.trim Removes whitespace from the start and end before storing it
html
<input v-model.lazy="name"> <!-- only updates once the user leaves the field --> <input v-model.number="age"> <!-- stores 21 rather than '21' --> <input v-model.trim="username"> <!-- ' john ' is stored as 'john' --> <input v-model.lazy.trim="x"> <!-- modifiers can be chained -->

Text inputs always produce strings, even when the user types digits, so without .number a comparison such as age.value > 18 compares a string against a number. If the input cannot be parsed as a number, .number leaves the original string in place. An <input type="number"> has .number applied automatically.

Changing the state from <script setup> (e.g. name.value = '...') updates the text shown in the field as well: the binding is genuinely two-way.

10.6Lists: v-for

What / when: render one element per item in an array (list, table rows, cards, <option>s) [Wk5 slides "List Rendering"].

vue
<script setup> const items1 = ref(['a', 'b', 'c']) const items2 = ref([{ message: 'Foo' }, { message: 'Bar' }]) const range = ref(10) const object = ref({ title: 'Foo', author: 'Bar', isbn: '12236' }) </script> <template> <li v-for="(item, idx) in items1">{{ idx }} - {{ item }}</li> <!-- optional index --> <li v-for="item in items2">{{ item.message }}</li> <!-- array of objects --> <span v-for="n in range">{{ n }}  </span> <!-- integer: repeats 1..10 --> <li v-for="(value, name, index) in object">{{ index }}. {{ name }}: {{ value }}</li> <!-- object: ORDER = value, name, index --> <!-- block of several elements per item --> <ul> <template v-for="item in items"> <li>{{ item.msg }}</li> <li class="divider">==========</li> </template> </ul> </template>

[wk5 Example7.vue, Example8.vue, Example9.vue].

Always add a unique :key so Vue tracks nodes correctly: v-for="product in products" :key="product.id". When there is no id, :key="index" is acceptable [Wk6 slides "Dynamic Properties (1)"; LT26 q3.vue uses Date.now()].

Table [wk5 Example10.vue]: data lives in a ref, the template just loops (clean separation of data and presentation).

html
<table class="table table-dark"><tbody> <tr v-for="dam in dams"><td>{{ dam.name }}</td><td>{{ dam.country }}</td><td>{{ dam.electricity }} MegaWatts</td></tr> </tbody></table>

Filtering and derived lists use computed (§7.12) so the template stays a plain v-for:

javascript
const evenNumbers = computed(() => numbers.value.filter(n => n % 2 === 0)) // [wk5 Example8.vue]

v-if and v-for on the same element. v-if has higher priority than v-for, so the v-if cannot see the loop variable and errors. Do not combine them; move v-for to a wrapping <template> [Wk5 slides "List Rendering (5)"]:

html
<template v-for="student in students"> <li v-if="student.isInDeanList">{{ student.name }}</li> </template>

Editing the list (Exercise 4 [wk5 Ex4.vue solution]): the data array is the single source of truth; change the array and the list re-renders.

vue
<li v-for="(item, i) in items">{{ item }} <button @click="items.splice(i, 1)">Delete!</button></li> <input @keyup.enter="add" v-model="newItem"> <button @click="add">Add!</button> <script setup> function add() { items.value.push(newItem.value); newItem.value = '' } </script>

Keys, and filtering with computed

Key: a unique identifier attached to each item in a v-for loop so Vue can track which rendered element corresponds to which underlying item as the list changes. Without a reliable key, when the list changes Vue cannot tell whether an item was added, removed or reordered, and may reuse the wrong rendered element for the wrong piece of data. Prefer a real id (user.id); avoid the index as the key if the list can be reordered or filtered.

index counts from 0 and is handy for display (numbering a list). Looping over an object gives the value, then the key: v-for="(value, key) in user".

Instead of v-if on the loop element, filter first with a computed property and leave the template a simple loop:

vue
<script setup> import { ref, computed } from 'vue' const fruits = ref(['Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry']) const filteredFruits = computed(() => fruits.value.filter(fruit => fruit !== 'Banana')) </script> <template> <li v-for="fruit in filteredFruits" :key="fruit">{{ fruit }}</li> </template>

This keeps the filtering logic in <script setup>, where it can be named, tested and reused.

lessons.subtitle: computed, watch, lifecycle hooks and localStorage.

🗺️ In this chapter
1computed, methods and watch→2Lifecycle hooks→3Saving data in the browser: localStorage→4Vue debugging 101
11.1computed, methods and watch

Computed property = a derived value that you use like a variable. It is cached and only recalculates when its reactive dependencies change [Wk5 slides "Computed Property"].

vue
<script setup> import { ref, computed } from 'vue' const fName = ref('Mike') const lName = ref('Jones') const fullName = computed(() => fName.value + ' ' + lName.value) // use .value inside function getFullName() { return fName.value + ' ' + lName.value } // method: re-runs on EVERY re-render </script> <template> <p>{{ fullName }}</p> <!-- computed: no () --> <p>{{ getFullName() }}</p> <!-- method: with () --> </template>

[wk5 Example3.vue].

computed method watch
Use for a value derived from other data (totals, filtered lists, class objects, disabled flags) actions triggered by events side effects when data changes (API call, DOM change)
Called in template without () in template with () or from @click automatically; you never call it
Cached? yes no n/a
Returns a value anything nothing needed

[Wk5 slides "Computed vs Methods"; Wk6 slides "Watchers"]. "Use computed whenever possible" [Wk5 take-away].

Keep computed functions pure (no assignments to other refs). The provided Ex3 solution [wk5 Ex3.vue] writes to lastResult inside computed; it works but is not a pattern to copy.

Watcher [wk6 Example8View.vue]: the first argument is the ref itself (not .value); the callback gets (newValue, oldValue) and may be async.

vue
<script setup> import { ref, watch } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'https://yesno.wtf/api' const question = ref('') const answer = ref('Questions usually contain a question mark. ;-)') async function getAnswer(newQuestion) { if (newQuestion.includes('?')) { answer.value = 'Thinking...' try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) answer.value = response.data.answer } catch (error) { answer.value = 'Error! Could not reach the API. ' + error } } } watch(question, getAnswer) </script> <template><input v-model="question"> <p>{{ answer }}</p></template>

computed in detail

computed: creates a reactive value derived from other reactive state, recalculated automatically whenever that state changes. It takes a function and returns a ref-like object whose .value holds the result: fullName.value in <script setup>, {{ fullName }} in the template.

The same result can come from an ordinary function, but behaves differently in caching:

javascript
function getFullName() { return firstName.value + ' ' + lastName.value }
computed A method call getFullName()
Recalculates when Only when the reactive state it depends on changes Every time the component re-renders
Result while unchanged Cached, reused instantly Recomputed from scratch each time

For string concatenation the difference is unnoticeable; for filtering or sorting a large list, recomputing on every render is wasteful.

Computed values are read-only by default. Assigning to one gives a runtime warning, because Vue cannot work backwards from a new full name to a new first and last name. firstName and lastName stay the source of truth; fullName only reflects them.

javascript
fullName.value = 'Grace Hopper' // warning: computed values are readonly

computed vs watch

computed cannot cleanly handle side effects (things that reach outside the component's own rendering: calling an API, writing to localStorage, imperative DOM work). For that, watch runs a callback whenever a specific piece of reactive state changes.

computed watch
Produces A new reactive value, used directly in the template No return value; runs arbitrary side-effecting code
Typical use Pure derivation: fullName from firstName + lastName Reacting to a change: calling an API, writing to localStorage, logging
Gets old/new values? No, it just recomputes Yes, the callback receives (newValue, oldValue)

Rule of thumb: derive with computed, react with watch.

11.2Lifecycle hooks

Functions that run at stages of a component's life [Wk5 slides "Lifecycle Hooks"]: created, mounted (DOM rendered), updated, unmounted. The course focuses only on onMounted.

javascript
import { onMounted } from 'vue' onMounted(() => { /* runs once after the component is inserted into the DOM */ }) onMounted(async () => { await getPosts() }) // async version [wk5 Example14.vue] onMounted(loadData) // pass an existing function [LT26 q4.vue]

Use it for: the initial API call, DOM access (focusing an input), initialising data from localStorage. onUnmounted is for cleanup (clearInterval, removing listeners).

The Wk5 slide names an onCreated(() => {...}) hook. That does not exist in Vue 3's Composition API. In <script setup> the code at the top already runs at "created" time; to run something after render use onMounted. The Extra Exercises PDFs also mention a created() hook; that is the Options API spelling (§7.16).

Lifecycle vocabulary and every hook

Lifecycle: the sequence of stages a component passes through, from creation to removal from the page. Lifecycle hook: a function that runs automatically at a specific stage. Vue calls it for you; you never invoke it from the template.

Hook Runs
onBeforeMount Just before the component is inserted into the page
onMounted Just after the component is inserted into the page
onBeforeUpdate Just before a reactive change updates the DOM
onUpdated Just after a reactive change has updated the DOM
onBeforeUnmount Just before the component is removed from the page
onUnmounted Just after the component is removed from the page

Each is imported from vue and accepts a single function.

onMounted is where DOM-dependent code goes. Code directly in <script setup> runs while the component is being set up, before it is attached to the page, so reading the page there fails:

vue
<script setup> import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue' const width = ref(0) onMounted(() => { width.value = window.innerWidth }) </script> <template><p>Window width: {{ width }}</p></template>

onUnmounted is for cleanup. Without it, the timer below would keep running in the background even after its component is gone:

vue
<script setup> import { onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue' let timer onMounted(() => { timer = setInterval(() => console.log('Tick'), 1000) }) onUnmounted(() => { clearInterval(timer) }) </script>

Memory leak: a resource (timer, event listener, subscription) that keeps running after it is no longer needed because nothing stopped it. Anything started in onMounted that does not stop on its own should be stopped in onUnmounted.

onUpdated runs after every reactive update, not once per specific piece of state. To react to one specific value changing, use watch.

vue
<script setup> import { onUpdated } from 'vue' onUpdated(() => { console.log('The DOM has just been updated') }) </script>

Order of execution for a single component with no children:

vue
<script setup> import { onBeforeMount, onMounted, onBeforeUpdate, onUpdated, onBeforeUnmount, onUnmounted } from 'vue' onBeforeMount(() => console.log('1: before mount')) onMounted(() => console.log('2: mounted')) onBeforeUpdate(() => console.log('3: before update')) onUpdated(() => console.log('4: updated')) onBeforeUnmount(() => console.log('5: before unmount')) onUnmounted(() => console.log('6: unmounted')) </script>

before mount and mounted run exactly once at the start. before update and updated run as a pair for every reactive change that affects the rendered output, so they may run many times or not at all. before unmount and unmounted run exactly once at the end.

11.3Saving data in the browser: localStorage

For data that must survive refresh or restart (draft notes, dark mode, language) [Wk6 slides "Persisting Data with Local Storage"]. It stores strings per origin (protocol + domain + port). Do not store passwords or API keys.

javascript
localStorage.setItem(key, value) // stores a STRING localStorage.getItem(key) // returns string or null localStorage.removeItem(key) // deletes it // objects and arrays: serialise then deserialise localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify({ theme: 'dark', fontSize: 16 })) const settings = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key))
vue
<script setup> import { ref, onMounted } from "vue" const STORAGE_KEY = "draft_note" const note = ref("") onMounted(() => { // load on start const saved = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY) if (saved !== null) note.value = saved }) function saveDraft() { localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, note.value) } function clearDraft() { note.value = ""; localStorage.removeItem(STORAGE_KEY) } </script> <template><textarea v-model="note" @input="saveDraft"></textarea><button @click="clearDraft">Clear Draft</button></template>

[wk6 Example7View.vue]. Settings panel pattern: save in @change / @input, load in onMounted, reset clears both the refs and the storage key, and the child emits the settings to the parent [wk6resource SettingPanel.vue, Ex5View.vue]. Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch so corrupted data cannot crash the app [State Management PDF, Tips].

11.4Vue debugging 101

Use the Chrome console and Vue devtools [Wk4 slides "Vue Debugging 101"].

Symptom Usual cause Fix
Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier typo, missing comma or brace, or a hidden strange character (often from pasted slide text with curly quotes) retype the line with straight quotes " '
[Vue warn]: Property or method "x" is not defined variable or function used in the template but never declared or returned declare it in <script setup>; check spelling and case
Button does nothing forgot .value in the handler, or wrote @click="fn()" when a call is not wanted see §7.9
Page never updates the variable is a plain const, not a ref wrap in ref()
List shows nothing v-for over an object where you have an array inside it drill into the array (§8.5 courseInfo)

If you hit something you cannot figure out, the official Vue forum (forum.vuejs.org/c/help) is a good next stop.

Take-away (Weeks 4 to 5): with vanilla JavaScript you constantly go back and forth between HTML and script via the DOM, searching from the root with document.getElement.... With Vue you declare the connection between HTML and script and focus on the logic: no more document.getElement.... Everywhere you would have written document.querySelector(...), Vue lets you write a directive or a binding instead.

🗺️ In this chapter
1Components: props, slots, emits→2Vue Router (client-side routing)→3Options API: recognise it, do not write it
12.1Components: props, slots, emits

What / why: split a page into small reusable, self-contained pieces (like your own HTML tags), each with its own template, logic and CSS [Wk6 slides "Components"].

Diagram: the data-flow rule.

#From → ToWhat happens
1Parent → Childprops: data goes DOWN :prod="product"
2Parent → Childslot content goes DOWN <AlertBox>text</AlertBox>
3Child → Parentemit an event with a payload, goes UP $emit('enlarge', 0.1)
4Parent → Parenthandler changes the parent state fontSize += amount

Read it as: parents talk to children through props and slots; children talk back through events. A child never edits parent data directly.

Define, import and use [Wk6 slides; wk6 Example1View.vue]:

vue
<!-- components/ButtonCounter.vue --> <script setup> import { ref } from 'vue' const count = ref(0) </script> <template> <button @click="count++">You clicked me {{ count }} times.</button> </template> <!-- views/Example1View.vue --> <script setup> import ButtonCounter from '../components/ButtonCounter.vue' // PascalCase name </script> <template> <ButtonCounter /> <!-- PascalCase works --> <button-counter /> <!-- kebab-case works in the template --> <!-- <buttoncounter /> --> <!-- does NOT work --> </template>

Naming: PascalCase for component names (valid JS identifiers; distinguishes from HTML tags). In <script setup> the import name must be PascalCase; import button-counter ... is invalid JavaScript. @/components/X.vue is an alias for src/components [wk6resource Ex4View.vue] (added context).

Where files go [Wk6 slides "src/components/ vs src/views/"]: If it is a page that has a URL, put it in views/. If it is a piece of UI you can reuse, put it in components/.

Props (parent to child) [Wk6 slides "Passing Props"]:

vue
<!-- components/Product.vue: declare --> <script setup> const props = defineProps(['name', 'price']) // array of names console.log(props.name) // JS: props.name </script> <template><h3>Product: {{ name }} | Price: {{ price }}</h3></template> <!-- template: just name --> <!-- object syntax with types (String, Number, Boolean, Object, Array) --> const props = defineProps({ greetingMessage: String }) <!-- parent: use as attributes; declare in camelCase, pass in kebab-case --> <Product name="iPhone" price="1000" /> <ChildComponent greeting-message="hello" />

[wk6 Example2View.vue]. Static vs dynamic: price="1000" passes the string "1000"; :price="1000" passes a number, and :prod="product" passes an object (added context).

Dynamic props with v-for [wk6 Example3View.vue, Product2.vue]:

vue
<!-- parent --> <Product v-for="product in products" v-bind:key="product.id" v-bind:prod="product" /> <!-- child --> <script setup> const props = defineProps({ prod: Object }) </script> <template><h3>{{ prod.id }} : {{ prod.name }}</h3></template>

Props flow one way; do not modify a prop inside the child (added context). To let the child request a change, use an event.

Slots (parent to child content) [wk6 Example4View.vue, AlertBox.vue, Book.vue]:

vue
<!-- AlertBox.vue (default slot) --> <template><div class="alert alert-warning"><slot></slot></div></template> <!-- use --> <AlertBox>This is a cool book: check it out!</AlertBox> <!-- Book.vue (named slots) --> <template><div><slot name="author"></slot><slot name="title"></slot></div></template> <!-- use --> <Book> <template v-slot:author><h3 style="color:red">{{ author }}</h3></template> <template v-slot:title><h3>{{ title }}</h3></template> </Book>

Use a slot when the parent should decide part of the child's content, for example Exercise 3 puts a Delete button into each BlogPost via a slot [Wk6 slides Exercise 3].

Emitting events (child to parent) [wk6 Product3.vue, Product4.vue, Example5View.vue, Example6View.vue]:

vue
<!-- child --> <script setup> const props = defineProps({ prod: Object }) const emit = defineEmits(['enlarge', 'shrink']) // declare events the child can emit function doShrink() { emit('shrink', { amount: 0.1 }) } // in a function: emit(name, payload) </script> <template> <button v-on:click="$emit('enlarge', 0.1)">Enlarge text</button> <!-- inline: $emit --> <button v-on:click="doShrink">Shrink text</button> </template> <!-- parent: listen exactly like an HTML event; the payload arrives as the handler's argument --> <script setup> const fontSize = ref(1) function onEnlarge(enlargeAmount) { fontSize.value += enlargeAmount } function onShrink(shrink) { fontSize.value -= shrink.amount } </script> <Product v-for="product in products" :key="product.id" :prod="product" @enlarge="onEnlarge" @shrink="onShrink" /> <!-- or inline: @enlarge="fontSize += 0.1" -->

Event names follow the same casing rule as props: emit('settings-changed', settings) is heard with @settings-changed="applySettings" [wk6resource SettingPanel.vue, Ex5View.vue]. Pass an index or id with the event so the parent knows which item: $emit('delete', idx) [wk6resource TaskTracker.vue].

Global registration [Wk6 slides "Global Registration"; wk6 main.js]: usable in any component without importing.

javascript
import TheWelcome from './components/TheWelcome.vue' app.component('TheWelcome', TheWelcome)

More on components

"Components allow us to split the UI into independent and reusable pieces, and think about each piece in isolation. It's common for an app to be organized into a tree of nested components."

A second simple example, a self-contained like counter that can be reused as many times as you like:

vue
<!-- components/ButtonCounter.vue --> <script setup> import { ref } from 'vue' const count = ref(0) </script> <template> <p>If you like my page, click </p> <button @click="count++">Like</button> <p>People liked me {{ count }} times.</p> <p v-if="count > 2"> I am POPU-LAR.</p> </template>
  • Intuitively, a component's tag is replaced by its own template at render time. A parent imports the child and references its tag.
  • Passing one object prop instead of many primitive props is especially useful when you do not know the exact shape or content ahead of time (data from user input or an async API request).
  • Declaring emitted events with defineEmits is recommended because it documents the component's public interface: anyone reading the <script setup> block can see the props it accepts and the events it can emit.
  • Props flow data down; a child never mutates a prop. To ask for a change, it emits an event.
  • Global registration trade-off: convenient for a small number of truly app-wide components (a base button, an icon set), but local imports keep each component's dependencies explicit and are preferred for everything else. A large app registered entirely globally makes it hard to tell from one file what it depends on.

Take-away (components): define reusable templates as components; use props and slots to pass data and markup in; use $emit / defineEmits with custom events (optionally carrying an argument) to pass data back out; use localStorage to persist non-sensitive data such as user preferences across page loads.

12.2Vue Router (client-side routing)

What / why: in a Single-Page App the router swaps components without reloading the page. Server-side routing (Express + ejs) reloads the whole page for each link [Wk4 slides "Routing (1)"].

javascript
// router/index.js import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router' import MainMenu from '../components/MainMenu.vue' const router = createRouter({ history: createWebHistory(import.meta.env.BASE_URL), routes: [ { path: '/', component: MainMenu }, { path: '/invalid', redirect: '/Example1' }, // static redirect { path: '/Example1/', component: Example1 }, { path: '/Example10/:name', component: Example10 }, // :name = route parameter ], }) export default router
html
<!-- links: use RouterLink, NOT <a href> (no page reload) --> <RouterLink to="/">Go to Home</RouterLink> <RouterLink to="/Example10/Jack">Example10</RouterLink> <!-- where the current route's component shows up: place ONCE, usually in App.vue --> <RouterView />

Read a route parameter [wk4 Example10.vue]:

vue
<script setup> import { useRoute } from 'vue-router' const route = useRoute() // 1. initialise the hook const username = route.params.name // 2. params are ALWAYS strings </script> <template><h1>Hello {{ username }}</h1></template>

Redirect from code [wk4 Example11.vue]:

vue
<script setup> import { useRouter } from "vue-router" const router = useRouter() function logout() { // logout logic ... router.push("/Example1") // changes the address and loads the mapped component } </script> <template><button @click="logout">Log Out?</button></template>

Use cases named on the slide: redirect to a default landing page; redirect to login after registration or to /products after log out.

The lab tests hide the router: each q1..q4 component is mapped to /q1..q4 by router/index.js and menu.vue links to them with <router-link to="/q1"> [LT26 router/index.js, menu.vue]. You only edit the qN file.

12.3Options API: recognise it, do not write it

Two provided files use the older style: data(), methods, props: [...], emits, this.$emit [wk6 Counter.vue, MyComp.vue]. Mapping (added context):

Options API <script setup> (what you write)
data() { return { value: 0 } } const value = ref(0)
methods: { modify(n) { this.value += n } } function modify(n) { value.value += n }
props: ['value'] defineProps(['value'])
emits: ['change'] + this.$emit('change', x) defineEmits(['change']) + emit('change', x)
created() {...} code at the top level of <script setup> (or onMounted)

lessons.title: Axios concepts
lessons.goal: Promises, the four methods, the response object and JSON shape.
lessons.subtitle: Promises, the four methods, the response object and JSON shape.
lessons.html:
🗺️ In this chapter
1What Axios is and why it is here→2Promises and async/await in 60 seconds→3The four methods: signatures and when to use…→4The response object→5Know your JSON shape before you assign it
13.1What Axios is and why it is here

An asynchronous request starts now and finishes later, so the page does not freeze while it waits for a server [Wk5 slides "Asynchronous Requests (1)"]. Vue itself has no HTTP library. Axios is a Promise-based HTTP client and "the recommended library for Vue"; it is similar to fetch from WAD1 [Wk5 slides]. Use it to fetch JSON, or to create/read/update/delete (CRUD) data on a REST server.

bash
pnpm add axios # once per project (already installed in the lab-test projects)
vue
import axios from 'axios' // at the top of <script setup>

Lab tests say: "Use Axios for all HTTP calls" and no other libraries (so no fetch, no jQuery) [LT26 Q4 instructions].

Axios or fetch? Axios is Promise-based like fetch, but parses JSON automatically and supports request/response interceptors. A Vue app running in the browser has no direct database access: it sends a request over the network to a server, which responds with data (typically JSON), and Axios is the tool that sends the request and receives the response.

13.2Promises and async/await in 60 seconds

A Promise stands for a value not yet known. It has three states [Wk5 slides "Understanding Callbacks, Promises, and Async/Await"]:

State Meaning What runs
Pending still in progress none yet
Fulfilled finished successfully the line after await
Rejected failed the catch block

Write every request like this (the style used in ALL the course examples):

javascript
async function getAdvice() { // "async" marks the function try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) // "await" pauses THIS function until the server replies advice.value = response.data.slip.advice // success path } catch (error) { advice.value = error.message // failure path (network down, 4xx, 5xx ...) } }

[wk5 Example11.vue].

  • await may only be used inside an async function. An onMounted callback that awaits must be async too.
  • An async function always returns a Promise.
  • Axios throws (rejects) for any non-2xx HTTP status (400, 404, 409, 500), so those land in catch. That is how "Error renting bike" is handled [LT24 Q4 Part D hint: "Handle the HTTP 400 error"].

async marks a function as one that can pause its own execution with await while it waits for a promise to resolve. axios.get(url) returns a promise that resolves when the server replies, and await pauses the surrounding function until then without blocking the rest of the page. The function passed to onMounted must be declared async to use await inside it:

vue
<script setup> import { onMounted } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'https://api.example.com/users' async function loadData() { try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) console.log(response.data) } catch (error) { console.error(error) } } onMounted(loadData) </script>
13.3The four methods: signatures and when to use them
Method Signature HTTP meaning Typical use Where data goes
GET axios.get(url[, config]) read load a list or one item query string via config.params
POST axios.post(url[, data[, config]]) create add a new item 2nd argument = body
PUT axios.put(url[, data[, config]]) replace / update an existing item edit an item by id 2nd argument = body; id in the URL
DELETE axios.delete(url[, config]) remove delete an item by id id in the URL; a body only via { data: {...} }

[Wk5 slides "Axios" and each method slide]. Note the argument positions: GET and DELETE have no data argument (config is 2nd); POST and PUT take data 2nd, config 3rd.

Diagram: one request, end to end (onMounted GET and a button-triggered POST).

#From → ToWhat happens
1Vue component → axiosonMounted: axios.get(url)
2axios → REST serverGET /posts
3Server → axios200 + JSON array
4axios → Vueresponse.data (await returns)
5Vue → Vueposts.value = response.data, template re-renders
6User → Vueclick Add (v-model already holds the inputs)
7Vue → axiosaxios.post(url, { subject, entry, mood })
8axios → ServerPOST /posts with a JSON body
9Server → axios201 + created item (or 400 / 409: axios THROWS)
10axios → Vueresponse.data (or the catch runs)
11Vue → Vueupdate state, or show an error message

Follow the arrows top to bottom. The key idea: the component never edits the DOM; it changes a ref and Vue re-renders. On a failure, execution jumps to catch.

13.4The response object

await axios.xxx(...) returns a response object [Wk5 slides "Axios Response Object"]:

Property Meaning Example
response.data the payload (parsed JSON becomes a JS object/array automatically) response.data.slip.advice
response.status HTTP code 200, 201
response.statusText HTTP message 'OK'
response.headers response headers content type, cookies

In catch (error): error.message is the readable message (used throughout the course). For the server's own error text and code use error.response.data and error.response.status (added context: not shown in the slides, but it is how you read a 4xx body; error.response is undefined when the server was unreachable).

Forgetting .data is one of the most common Axios mistakes. response itself is not the data requested; it is a wrapper containing that data alongside the status code and headers. Storing response in a ref instead of response.data produces a value the rest of the component cannot use as expected.

13.5Know your JSON shape before you assign it

response.data is whatever the server sent. Look at the JSON, then drill in.

Server GET returns So assign
Blog (http://localhost:8000/posts) [wk5 posts.json] an array [ {id, subject, entry, mood}, ... ] posts.value = response.data
CourseInfo (http://127.0.0.1:8000/api) [LT26 courses.json, server.js] an object { "courseInfo": [ ... ] } courses.value = response.data.courseInfo
Bike stations (http://localhost:8000/api) [LT24 bike_stations.json] an array [ {id, name, available_bikes, available_docks} ] stations.value = response.data
Advice [wk5 Example11.vue] { slip: { advice: "..." } } response.data.slip.advice
OpenWeatherMap [wk5 Example12.vue] { weather: [ {description} ], main: { temp } } response.data.weather[0].description, response.data.main.temp

The 2026 Q4 trap: the question says "assign the returned JSON object to courses", but the template does v-for="course in courses" and reads course.code. The JSON is { "courseInfo": [...] }. If you assign the whole object, the table stays empty (v-for over an object iterates its values, giving one row with an array). Use response.data.courseInfo. Tip: put console.log(response.data) first and read the DevTools console.

lessons.title: Axios CRUD
lessons.goal: GET, POST, PUT and DELETE with worked code.
lessons.subtitle: GET, POST, PUT and DELETE with worked code.
lessons.html:
🗺️ In this chapter
1GET→2POST→3PUT→4DELETE
14.1GET

Read data. GET has no body; send parameters in config.params, which Axios turns into ?name=value&... [Wk5 slides "Axios: GET method"; wk5 Example12.vue].

vue
<script setup> import axios from 'axios' import { ref } from 'vue' const API_URL = 'https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather' const weatherData = ref('') const temperature = ref('') const status = ref('Ready to fetch weather data') async function getData() { try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL, { params: { q: 'Singapore,sg', APPID: 'YOUR_KEY', units: 'metric' }, // becomes ?q=Singapore,sg&APPID=...&units=metric }) weatherData.value = response.data.weather[0].description temperature.value = response.data.main.temp status.value = 'Data received successfully!' } catch (error) { status.value = 'Error fetching data!' weatherData.value = error.message } } </script> <template> <p>{{ status }}</p> <p>Weather: {{ weatherData }}, {{ temperature }}°C</p> <button type="button" @click="getData">Get Weather Data</button> </template>

Get one item by id: put the id in the path (GET /posts/:id): axios.get('http://localhost:8000/posts/' + id) (or a template string ${API_URL}/${id}) [Wk5 slides "A Blog Service"].

Load when the page opens: call it in onMounted [wk5 Example13.vue]:

vue
<script setup> import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/posts' const posts = ref([]) // start with an EMPTY array, never undefined async function loadData() { try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) posts.value = response.data // an array; Vue re-renders the table } catch (error) { posts.value = [{ entry: 'There was an error: ' + error.message }] // simple error display used in the course } } onMounted(loadData) </script> <template> <table class="table"> <thead><tr><th>Subject</th><th>Entry</th><th>Mood</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr v-for="post in posts" :key="post.id"> <td>{{ post.subject }}</td><td>{{ post.entry }}</td><td>{{ post.mood }}</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> </template>

The exam pattern is the same but with a named function (onMounted(loadData)) so the function can be re-used to refresh after a POST or DELETE [LT26 q4.vue; LT24 q4.vue rentBike calls getStations again].

Loading and error states

A request takes time and can fail, so a component should track both rather than assume data is present immediately:

vue
<script setup> import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'https://api.example.com/users' const users = ref([]) const isLoading = ref(true) const error = ref(null) async function loadData() { try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) users.value = response.data } catch (error) { error.value = 'Failed to load users' } finally { isLoading.value = false } } onMounted(loadData) </script> <template> <p v-if="isLoading">Loading...</p> <p v-else-if="error">{{ error }}</p> <ul v-else> <li v-for="user in users" :key="user.id">{{ user.name }}</li> </ul> </template>
Block Runs
try Attempts the request
catch Only if the request fails (network unavailable, error status); records a message instead of letting the failure go unnoticed
finally Always, exactly once, whether it succeeded or failed; the reliable place to turn off a loading indicator

Every method (get, post, put, patch, delete) returns a promise, is typically awaited inside an async function, and benefits from try / catch / finally. axios.patch(url, body) updates part of existing data and has the same shape as put.

14.2POST

Create data. Pass a plain JavaScript object as the 2nd argument; Axios sends it as JSON with Content-Type: application/json [Wk5 slides "Axios: POST method"].

vue
<script setup> import axios from 'axios' import { ref } from 'vue' const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/posts' const moods = ref(['Happy', 'Sad', 'Angry']) const subject = ref('') // one ref per input, bound with v-model const entry = ref('') const mood = ref('') const showStatus = ref(false) const status = ref('') async function add() { const data = { subject: subject.value, entry: entry.value, mood: mood.value } // keys must match what the server expects try { const response = await axios.post(API_URL, data) showStatus.value = true status.value = response.data } catch (error) { showStatus.value = true status.value = 'There was an error: ' + error.message } } </script> <template> Subject: <input type="text" v-model="subject" required><br> Entry: <textarea v-model="entry" cols="80" rows="5" required></textarea><br> Mood: <select v-model="mood"><option v-for="m in moods">{{ m }}</option></select><br> <button v-on:click="add">Submit New Post</button> <p v-if="showStatus">{{ status }}</p> </template>

[wk5 solution Ex5.vue]. Blog server: POST /posts returns 201 with the created post (including its new id) [wk5 posts.controller.js].

Field names come from the server, not the docs. Blog API.docx shows title / content, but the running posts.controller.js requires subject / entry / mood (and returns 400 if missing). Send what the code / JSON uses. Always read the JSON or the Postman example first.

After a successful POST, update the UI. Two options:

  1. Push the returned item (no extra request): courses.value.push(response.data.item). The CourseInfo server returns { message, item } [LT26 server.js].
  2. Re-fetch the list: await loadData() (simple, always correct; the bike lab does this).
14.3PUT

Update an existing item. Put the id in the URL and the new data in the body. The course describes PUT as replacing a resource (or creating it if absent) [Wk5 slides "Axios: PUT method"].

vue
<script setup> import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/posts' const posts = ref([]) const newEntry = ref('') const newMood = ref('') const toUpdate = ref(null) // the post being edited; null = no edit form shown const status = ref('') async function getPosts() { /* axios.get as in 5.6 */ } onMounted(getPosts) async function updatePost(id, subject) { try { const url = `${API_URL}/${id}` // id in the path const response = await axios.put(url, { // body: the FULL new record subject: subject, entry: newEntry.value, mood: newMood.value }) status.value = 'Update Successful' toUpdate.value = null // hide the form } catch (error) { status.value = 'There was an error: ' + error.message } await getPosts() // refresh the table } </script> <template> <p v-if="status != ''">{{ status }}</p> <tr v-for="post in posts" :key="post.id"> <td>{{ post.subject }}</td> <td><button class="btn btn-danger" v-on:click="toUpdate = post">Update</button></td> </tr> <div v-if="toUpdate"> <p>Subject: {{ toUpdate.subject }}</p> <input type="text" v-model="newEntry"> <select v-model="newMood"><option value="Happy">Happy</option><option value="Sad">Sad</option></select> <button v-on:click="updatePost(toUpdate.id, toUpdate.subject)">Update</button> </div> </template>

[wk5 Example14.vue]. Pattern: clicking Update on a row stores that row in toUpdate; v-if="toUpdate" reveals the edit form; the form's button calls updatePost.

PUT vs PATCH (added context): the blog server implements both PUT /posts/:id (all three fields required, replaces) and PATCH /posts/:id (any subset) [wk5 posts.routes.js, posts.controller.js]. The CourseInfo PUT behaves like a partial update (only changes fields that are sent) [LT26 server.js]. The syntax axios.patch(url, data) is identical (the slides do not cover it).

14.4DELETE

Remove an item. The id usually goes in the URL. DELETE takes no data argument; if you must send a body, wrap it as { data: {...} } in the config [Wk5 slides "Axios: DELETE method"].

vue
<script setup> const API_URL = 'http://localhost:8000/posts' async function deletePost(id, subject) { // optimistic UI update: remove locally first (as in the course example) let idx = 0 for (let post of posts.value) { if (post.subject == subject) { posts.value.splice(idx, 1); break } idx++ } try { const url = `${API_URL}/${id}` const response = await axios.delete(url, { data: { subject: subject } }) // body goes in config.data console.log(response.data) } catch (error) { console.log('There was an error: ' + error.message) } } </script> <template> <button class="btn btn-danger" v-on:click="deletePost(post.id, post.subject)">Delete</button> </template>

[wk5 Example15.vue]. Exercise 3 of Week 6 uses the same call with axios.delete(url, { data: { subject: subject } }) [Wk6 slides Exercise 3].

Two ways to remove the row after DELETE: posts.value = posts.value.filter(p => p.id !== id) (clean, no loop) or re-fetch with await getPosts(). The CourseInfo server needs only the course code in the URL (DELETE /api/:id, no body) and answers 404 if the code does not exist [LT26 server.js, Q4 Part C].

lessons.title: Axios patterns
lessons.goal: Headers, .env keys, CORS, the full CRUD skeleton and a mini project.
lessons.subtitle: Headers, .env keys, CORS, the full CRUD skeleton and a mini project.
lessons.html:
🗺️ In this chapter
1Request headers and other config→2CORS (why your call may be blocked)→3Full CRUD skeleton (copy this pattern)→4Axios checklist→5Mini project: user directory
15.1Request headers and other config

The last argument (the config) also carries headers, for example an auth token [Wk5 slides "Axios: Request Headers"]:

javascript
const config = { headers: { 'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN', 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } } const response = await axios.post(url, data, config) // data 2nd, config 3rd

Server side (Express) reads them with request.header("Authorization"). For GET/DELETE the config is the 2nd argument: axios.get(url, { headers: {...}, params: {...} }).

API keys & .env

Keys never go in the code you share. Vite reads .env in the project root and exposes only names that start with VITE_; restart pnpm dev after editing it.

javascript
# .env VITE_OPENWEATHER_API_KEY=YOUR_API_KEY_HERE
javascript
const API_KEY = import.meta.env.VITE_OPENWEATHER_API_KEY const API_URL = 'https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather' // Preferred: axios builds and URL-encodes the query string for you const response = await axios.get(API_URL, { params: { q: city, units: 'metric', appid: API_KEY } }) // If you build the string yourself, encode user text (spaces, &, ?) const url = `${API_URL}?q=${encodeURIComponent(city)}&units=metric&appid=${API_KEY}`
15.2CORS (why your call may be blocked)

The browser blocks a page on localhost:5173 from reading responses from localhost:8000 unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. The blog server does this with the cors() middleware [wk5 server.js], and the CourseInfo server sets the headers manually and answers the OPTIONS pre-flight [LT26 server.js]. You do not change the server in the lab test. If you see a CORS error, the server is either not running or on a different port/URL than your API_URL.

15.3Full CRUD skeleton (copy this pattern)
House style used by every Axios example in this file
PartWriteNot
Requesta named async function with try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) … } catch (error) { … }.then() / .catch() chains
URLconst API_URL = '…' once at the top; `${API_URL}/${id}` for idsconst url inside every function; url + id
Namesresponse, errorres, r, e, err
Reading dataconst response = await axios.get(…) then response.data(await axios.get(…)).data
On page loadonMounted(loadData)onMounted(async () => { … })
From the template@click="addItem", or @click="deleteItem(item.id)" when you pass an argument@click="addItem()"
After a writeawait loadData() (re-fetch) or update the local arrayleaving the table stale
Formatno semicolons, single quotes, 2-space indent
vue
<script setup> import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api' const items = ref([]) const errorMessage = ref('') const newName = ref('') // declare a ref for EVERY form field async function loadData() { // R errorMessage.value = '' try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) items.value = response.data // or response.data.someKey } catch (error) { errorMessage.value = 'Failed to load data' } } async function addItem() { // C errorMessage.value = '' try { const response = await axios.post(API_URL, { name: newName.value }) items.value.push(response.data.item) newName.value = '' // clear the form } catch (error) { errorMessage.value = 'Failed to add' } } async function updateItem(id) { // U try { await axios.put(`${API_URL}/${id}`, { name: newName.value }) await loadData() } catch (error) { errorMessage.value = 'Failed to update' } } async function deleteItem(id) { // D try { await axios.delete(`${API_URL}/${id}`) items.value = items.value.filter(i => i.id !== id) } catch (error) { errorMessage.value = 'Failed to delete' } } onMounted(loadData) </script> <template> <p v-if="errorMessage" class="error-msg">{{ errorMessage }}</p> <input v-model="newName"> <button @click="addItem">Add</button> <ul><li v-for="item in items" :key="item.id">{{ item.name }} <button @click="deleteItem(item.id)">Delete</button></li></ul> </template>

(The skeleton is my synthesis of the course patterns; each line follows [wk5 Example13/14/15, LT26 q4.vue].)

Promise.all for parallel GETs

To load one request per item, map the array to calls and wait for all of them inside an async function: they run at the same time, and it continues when the last one finishes.

javascript
async function fetchWeather(city) { // one request, with its own try/catch try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL, { params: { q: city.name, units: 'metric', appid: API_KEY } }) city.temp = Math.round(response.data.main.temp) } catch (error) { city.tempError = true } } async function fetchAllWeather() { await Promise.all(cities.value.map((city) => fetchWeather(city))) }
15.4Axios checklist
Check Why
import axios from 'axios' present otherwise axios is not defined
Function is async, calls use await otherwise you get a Promise, not data
Inside try { } catch (error) { } non-2xx and network errors throw
Server running and URL/port correct "Failed to load" usually means the server is off [LT26 Q4]
response.data drilled to the right level see §8.5
POST/PUT body keys match server field names server returns 400 otherwise
.value used when writing refs in script otherwise the UI does not update
Refresh or update local array after write table must show the change without a reload
Nothing hard-coded (messages, ids, data) lab rule "Do NOT hardcode" [LT26 Q4]; the alert text should come from response.data.message [LT24 Q4 Part C]
Same shape every time: API_URL, response, error, named async function, no .then() see the house-style table in §8.12
15.5Mini project: user directory

Combines ref, computed, v-model, v-for, v-if, :class, @click, onMounted, Axios and the Bootstrap grid, cards, forms and alerts.

vue
<script setup> import { ref, computed, onMounted } from 'vue' import axios from 'axios' const API_URL = 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users' const users = ref([]) const search = ref('') const isLoading = ref(true) const error = ref(null) const favourites = ref([]) const filteredUsers = computed(() => users.value.filter(u => u.name.toLowerCase().includes(search.value.toLowerCase())) ) function toggleFavourite(id) { favourites.value = favourites.value.includes(id) ? favourites.value.filter(f => f !== id) : [...favourites.value, id] } async function loadData() { try { const response = await axios.get(API_URL) users.value = response.data } catch (error) { error.value = 'Failed to load users' } finally { isLoading.value = false } } onMounted(loadData) </script> <template> <div class="container py-4"> <h1 class="mb-3">User Directory</h1> <input v-model.trim="search" class="form-control mb-4" placeholder="Search by name…"> <div v-if="isLoading" class="text-center"><div class="spinner-border"></div></div> <div v-else-if="error" class="alert alert-danger">{{ error }}</div> <p v-else-if="filteredUsers.length === 0" class="text-muted">No matches.</p> <div v-else class="row row-cols-1 row-cols-md-3 g-3"> <div v-for="user in filteredUsers" :key="user.id" class="col"> <div class="card h-100" :class="{ 'border-warning': favourites.includes(user.id) }"> <div class="card-body"> <h5 class="card-title">{{ user.name }}</h5> <p class="card-text text-muted">{{ user.email }}</p> <button class="btn btn-sm" :class="favourites.includes(user.id) ? 'btn-warning' : 'btn-outline-warning'" @click="toggleFavourite(user.id)" > {{ favourites.includes(user.id) ? '★ Favourite' : '☆ Favourite' }} </button> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </template>

lessons.title: Express & MongoDB
lessons.goal: Routes, controllers, models, REST design, Mongoose and EJS.
lessons.subtitle: Routes, controllers, models, REST design, Mongoose and EJS.
lessons.html:
🗺️ In this chapter
1Backend: Node, Express and MongoDB→2Express App Structure — the Routes/Controlle…→3REST API Design — HTTP Verbs & Status Codes→4CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)→5The Blog API Contract (from Blog API.docx)→6MongoDB + Mongoose→7EJS — Server-Rendered Views
16.1Backend: Node, Express and MongoDB
Chapter overview

Two parallel backend implementations are provided for the same "Blog Service," so you can compare a simple file-based approach against a real database:

javascript
wk5/server/blog/ → Node.js + Express.js, data persisted to a JSON file wk5/server/blog-with-mongodb/ → Node.js + Express.js + Mongoose + MongoDB Atlas (cloud)

Both expose the same REST API shape (see §10.4), which is the point — the frontend Vue code barely needs to change no matter which backend is running underneath it.

16.2Express App Structure — the Routes/Controllers/Model Pattern

Both backends follow a clean 3-layer separation of concerns:

javascript
server.js → wires everything together, starts listening routes/*.routes.js → maps a URL + HTTP verb to a controller function controllers/*.controller.js → the business logic + request/response handling model/*.model.js → the actual data access (file I/O or database queries)

server.js (file-based version):

javascript
const express = require("express"); const postsRoutes = require("./routes/posts.routes"); const server = express(); server.use(express.json()); // middleware: parses incoming JSON request bodies into req.body const cors = require('cors'); server.use(cors()); // adds Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * so the Vue dev server can call this API server.use("/posts", postsRoutes); // all routes under /posts are handled by postsRoutes // centralized error-handling middleware — catches anything passed to next(err) server.use((err, req, res, next) => { console.error(err); res.status(500).json({ error: "Internal server error" }); }); server.listen(8000, () => console.log(`API running on http://localhost:8000`));

routes/posts.routes.js — maps HTTP verb + path to a controller function:

javascript
const router = express.Router(); router.get("/", controller.listPosts); router.get("/:id", controller.getPostById); router.post("/", controller.createPost); router.put("/:id", controller.replacePost); router.patch("/:id", controller.updatePost); router.delete("/:id", controller.deletePost); module.exports = router;

controllers/posts.controller.js — validates input, calls the model, shapes the HTTP response:

javascript
exports.createPost = async (req, res, next) => { try { const { subject, entry, mood } = req.body || {}; if (typeof subject !== "string" || !subject.trim()) { return res.status(400).json({ error: "subject is required" }); // 400 = bad request (client error) } const created = await postsModel.create({ subject: subject.trim(), entry, mood: mood.trim() }); res.status(201).json(created); // 201 = "Created" — the correct status for a successful POST } catch (e) { next(e); // hands off to the error-handling middleware above } };

model/posts.model.js (file-based storage) — reads/writes a JSON file as the "database":

javascript
const fs = require("fs/promises"); async function readPosts() { try { const raw = await fs.readFile(DATA_FILE, "utf8"); return JSON.parse(raw); } catch (err) { if (err.code === "ENOENT") return []; // file doesn't exist yet → treat as empty throw err; } } exports.create = async ({ subject, entry, mood }) => { const posts = await readPosts(); const nextId = posts.reduce((max, p) => Math.max(max, p.id || 0), 0) + 1; // auto-increment ID const post = { id: nextId, subject, entry, mood }; posts.push(post); await fs.writeFile(DATA_FILE, JSON.stringify(posts, null, 2), "utf8"); return post; };

💡 Why this layered structure matters: the controller never touches the filesystem directly, and the routes never contain business logic. If you later swap the file-based model for a MongoDB model (exactly what blog-with-mongodb does), the routes and controllers barely change — only model/*.js is rewritten. This is the same "separation of concerns" idea CSS brings to HTML, now applied to backend architecture.

16.3REST API Design — HTTP Verbs & Status Codes
Verb Purpose Typical success status
GET Retrieve (no side effects) 200 OK
POST Create a new resource 201 Created
PUT Full replace of an existing resource (must supply all fields) 200 OK
PATCH Partial update (only supplied fields change) 200 OK
DELETE Remove a resource 200 OK
Status code Meaning
200 OK
201 Created (typical response to a successful POST)
400 Bad Request — client sent invalid/missing data
404 Not Found — the resource (e.g. that id) doesn't exist
500 Internal Server Error — something broke on the server side

PUT vs PATCH — the distinction that trips people up: the file-based controller's replacePost (PUT) requires subject, entry, and mood all be present (it's a full replace — missing fields would wipe them out). Its updatePost (PATCH) only validates fields that were actually supplied (subject !== undefined && ...), leaving the rest untouched.

16.4CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

Your Vue dev server typically runs on one port (e.g. localhost:5173) while your API runs on another (localhost:8000) — browsers block this kind of cross-origin request by default for security. The cors middleware explicitly tells the browser "this API allows requests from other origins":

javascript
server.use(cors()); // simplest form: allow ALL origins — fine for coursework, NOT for production

The MongoDB version shows a more locked-down, production-style pattern — only allowing specific origin patterns:

javascript
const allowedLocalhost = /^http:\/\/localhost(:\d+)?$/; server.use(cors({ origin: (origin, callback) => { if (!origin) return callback(null, true); // allow non-browser tools (Postman/curl) — they don't send an Origin header if (allowedLocalhost.test(origin)) return callback(null, true); return callback(new Error("Not allowed by CORS")); }, methods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"], }));
16.5The Blog API Contract (from Blog API.docx)

This is the exact contract the Vue frontend (Example13/14/15.vue, Ex5.vue) codes against:

Operation Path Method Success response
Create /posts/ POST 201 + the created post (with new id)
Retrieve all /posts/ GET 200 + array of posts
Retrieve one /posts/:id GET 200 + the post, or 404 if not found
Update (full) /posts/:id PUT 200 + updated post; 400 if a required field is missing
Update (partial) /posts/:id PATCH 200 + updated post — only supplied fields change
Delete /posts/:id DELETE 200 + the deleted post, or 404 if not found

Every error response follows the same shape: { "error": "<message>" } — a consistent envelope makes frontend error handling simpler (error.message or response.data.error is always where the message lives).

16.6MongoDB + Mongoose

Why MongoDB (a document database) instead of tabular rows: documents store field-value pairs directly (often as JSON/BSON) rather than fixed rows/columns, and different documents in the same collection don't need identical fields — the schema is flexible by default (though Mongoose lets you optionally enforce structure on top).

javascript
Database (e.g. "week10") └── Collection (e.g. "books") ← a group of similar documents └── Document (e.g. one book) ← { title: "...", isbn: "...", rating: 4.5, price: 20 }

Mongoose is an Object Data Modeling (ODM) library that sits between your Express app and raw MongoDB, giving you: - Schemas — define expected fields, types, defaults, and validation rules. - Models — a class representing a whole collection; an instance of a model = one document. - Convenience methods for CRUD instead of writing raw MongoDB query syntax.

Defining a schema and model:

javascript
const mongoose = require('mongoose'); const bookSchema = new mongoose.Schema({ title: { type: String, required: [true, 'A book must have a title'] }, isbn: { type: String, required: [true, 'A book must have an isbn'], unique: true }, rating: { type: Number, default: 3.0 }, price: { type: Number, required: [true, 'A book must have a price'] } }); const Book = mongoose.model('Book', bookSchema, 'books'); // 3rd arg pins the exact collection name exports.retrieveAll = function() { return Book.find(); }; // Model.find() with no filter = get everything

required: [true, 'message'] is a two-element array: a boolean flag and the validation error message shown if the field is missing.

Connecting to MongoDB Atlas (cloud):

javascript
const mongoose = require('mongoose'); const dotenv = require('dotenv'); dotenv.config({ path: './config.env' }); // loads variables from config.env into process.env async function connectDB() { try { await mongoose.connect(process.env.DB); // process.env.DB comes from config.env, NEVER hard-coded console.log("MongoDB connected successfully"); } catch (error) { console.error("MongoDB connection failed:", error.message); process.exit(1); } } function startServer() { server.listen(8000, "localhost", () => console.log(`Server running at http://localhost:8000/`)); } async function main() { await connectDB(); // IMPORTANT: wait for the DB connection first startServer(); // only start the server AFTER the DB connection succeeds } main();

config.env — the connection string, kept out of source code:

javascript
DB=mongodb+srv://<USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>@<CLUSTERADDRESS>/<DBNAME>?retryWrites=true&w=majority

🚨 Security note: environment variables exist specifically so secrets (DB passwords, API keys) never get hard-coded into .js files that might be committed to Git. config.env should be listed in .gitignore in any real project. (The sample config.env included in this course's zip has a live-looking connection string checked in — treat that as course-lab convenience only, never as the pattern to follow in your own project's repository.)

Connection string parameters: | Parameter | Purpose | |---|---| | retryWrites=true | Automatically retries a write once if a transient network error occurs | | w=majority | Write concern — the write must be acknowledged by a majority of replica-set members before being considered successful (durability guarantee) |

CRUD with Mongoose (from blog-with-mongodb):

javascript
exports.retrieveAll = () => Blog.find(); // GET all exports.findById = (id) => Blog.findOne({ id: id }); // GET one exports.addBlog = (id, subject, entry, mood) => Blog.create({ id, subject, entry, mood }); // POST exports.editBlog = (id, subject, entry, mood) => Blog.updateOne({ id }, { subject, entry, mood }); // PUT exports.deleteBlog = (id) => Blog.deleteOne({ id: id }); // DELETE

Note Blog.updateOne(...) and Blog.deleteOne(...) return a result object ({ modifiedCount, ... } / { deletedCount, ... }) rather than the document itself — the controller checks success.modifiedCount === 1 / success.deletedCount === 1 to confirm the operation actually changed something before reporting success.

Mongoose middleware (pre hooks) — auto-updating a timestamp on every save, without the caller having to remember to do it:

javascript
blogSchema.pre("save", function (next) { this.updateTimestamp = new Date(); next(); });
16.7EJS — Server-Rendered Views

Used in the mongodb_guide example to render a plain HTML page directly from the server (as opposed to the Vue-driven frontends used everywhere else in the course):

javascript
server.set("view engine", "ejs"); res.render("display-book", { bookList }); // renders views/display-book.ejs, injecting `bookList`
html
<!-- views/display-book.ejs --> <% if (bookList.length === 0) { %> <p>No books yet.</p> <% } else { %> <% bookList.forEach(book => { %> <p>Title: <%= book.title %></p> <% }); %> <% } %>

<% %> runs arbitrary JS (control flow, loops) without outputting anything; <%= %> evaluates an expression and injects its (HTML-escaped) result into the page. This is conceptually the server-side ancestor of what v-for/v-if do client-side in Vue — the difference is where the HTML gets generated (server, before the response is sent, vs. client, in the browser after data arrives via Axios).
